profile.summary: This is a dose extrapolation test on the Sci-Plex chemical transcriptomics data. For each of twelve cell line and drug pairs, three cancer cell lines crossed with four HDAC inhibitors, the cells treated at the drug's highest dose are held out, and a model must predict the single-cell expression distribution at that dose from control cells, the lower doses of the same drug and all doses of the other drugs in the same cell line. Expression is reduced to 50 marker genes chosen from the training conditions only. The protocol and the preprocessing come from the Generative Intervention Models paper and its codebase; the record holds the version reported by the PerturbPFN paper, which scores predictions by mean distance, gene-wise Pearson correlation and a 2-Wasserstein distance between the predicted and observed cell distributions.
profile.summary_source_locator: PerturbPFN: Section 4.2 and Appendix D.1 to D.3; GIM: Appendix D.2

summary_quotes.text: We evaluate perturbation-response prediction on the Sci-Plex single-cell drug perturbation dataset [20], using the highest-dosage holdout protocol of Schneider et al. [4].
The benchmark contains three cell lines, A549, K562, and MCF7, and four small-molecule perturbations, belinostat, dacinostat, givinostat, and quisinostat 2HCl, giving 3 × 4 = 12 held-out protocols.

For each protocol, the highest-dose response is held out, while the model receives lower doses of the same drug and all observed doses of the remaining drugs. It must predict the held-out cell distribution without observing drug targets or updating model parameters.
Cells are normalized to the median count of control cells, filtered, log-transformed, and restricted to a protocol-specific set of 50 marker genes selected using only the training conditions.

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: The question is whether a model can predict what a drug does to cells at a dose it has not seen, without being told the drug's target. Each test case gives the model the control cells, the same drug at lower doses and the other drugs at all doses, then asks for the distribution of expression vectors at the highest dose. The PerturbPFN authors describe this as dose extrapolation under unknown perturbation targets, and point out that the held-out drug is not wholly unseen because its lower doses are in the context. Because the prediction is a distribution over cells rather than a mean, the scoring can catch a model that gets the direction of the response right but the magnitude wrong.

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The data are the Sci-Plex single-cell drug perturbation data of Srivatsan et al., restricted by the GIM authors to four drugs of the epigenetic regulation pathway in three human cancer cell lines, A549, K562 and MCF7, which gives twelve cell line and drug settings. The GIM preprocessing script lists the four drugs as dacinostat, givinostat, belinostat and quisinostat 2HCl and the doses as 0, 10, 100, 1000 and 10000, with 10000 as the held-out dose. Cells are normalised to the median count of the unperturbed cells, cells with fewer than 200 counts and genes expressed in fewer than 20 cells are dropped, counts are log transformed, then the top 1000 highly variable genes are taken and reduced to 50 marker genes. The script computes both of those steps on the training data only, scoring every gene against control for each drug with a Wilcoxon test ranked by absolute score, then keeping the 50 genes with the largest sum of absolute scores across the drugs, using the training cells only, so the gene set is specific to each held-out protocol. A code comment says it selects the genes most often among the top 50 marker genes, but the code sums the absolute scores and does not use that count. Perturbation features are one-hot drug and dose codes plus a rescaled dose value, and control cells form the observational regime. The GIM paper states that holding out the highest dose leaves 16 perturbations for training in each setting.

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A method predicts a set of cells for the held-out condition. Three metrics are computed per protocol. Mean distance is the Euclidean distance between the predicted and true mean response, lower is better. Pearson correlation measures gene-wise agreement between those mean responses, higher is better. The 2-Wasserstein distance compares the whole predicted and observed cell distributions, approximated by a debiased entropic Sinkhorn cost with squared Euclidean ground cost, epsilon 0.1, at most 200 iterations and tolerance 10 to the minus 6, computed on equally sized deterministically sampled cell sets, lower is better. For the table, each metric is oriented so that higher is better and min-max normalised across the models being compared within each protocol, then averaged over the twelve protocols, and the three columns are averaged for the overall rank. The PerturbPFN authors say plainly that these normalised scores depend on which models are in the comparison, and give the raw per-protocol distributions only as box plots in a figure. All methods are evaluated on the same held-out cells with the same metric code, and metrics for the baselines were recomputed with that code where prediction arrays were available.

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The protocol lives in the GIM repository. Create its conda environment, install the package and the bundled cdt source, download the raw Sci-Plex files into data/sciplex/raw, then run the preprocessing script once per cell line, which produces the twelve data sets with their train and test splits. The repository's shell scripts then run GIM and the baselines on the single-cell data, and a notebook makes the figures. The PerturbPFN paper publishes no code of its own, so its own model cannot be run from the sources read here.
